entities.summary:
Stephen Hopkins (1707–1785) was a pivotal figure in the American Revolution and a prominent statesman of Rhode Island, whose career spanned nearly five decades of colonial and early national politics. As a signer of the Declaration of Independence and the Continental Association, and a long-serving governor of the Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, Hopkins championed colonial self-governance and economic independence against escalating British imperial policies. His intellectual contributions, notably through his influential pamphlet 'The Rights of Colonies Examined,' articulated core arguments for American sovereignty, positioning him as a vital voice in the nascent movement for independence.

Hopkins's political life began in 1732 as a representative to the General Assembly from Scituate, Rhode Island, where he quickly rose through the ranks, serving as Speaker of the House. He first assumed the governorship in 1755, a position he held for nine non-consecutive terms, navigating the complex political landscape between local factions and imperial demands. A key achievement during his tenure was the successful negotiation of the boundary dispute with Connecticut in 1752. Later, as a delegate to the Continental Congresses from 1774 to 1776, Hopkins actively participated in the debates leading to the Declaration of Independence, famously declaring 'My hand trembles, but my heart does not' as he signed the document despite severe palsy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Stephen Hopkins was a key figure in the American Revolution, serving as a long-term governor of Rhode Island and signing the Declaration of Independence, thereby contributing directly to the founding of the United States. His influential writings and political leadership helped galvanize colonial resistance to British rule.
